name: Purépecha
variant: P'urhépecha of the Meseta and the Lake
summary: Aspect, tense and person suffixes added to the root, one after another.

conjugator.label: Verb
conjugator.hint: Type the verb in the infinitive (with -ni) or just the root: uandani «speak», t'ireni «eat», ch'anani «play». Accents are optional; if you type them, they are kept.

own.hint: Type any verb in the infinitive and its meaning in English. We conjugate it by adding the suffixes to the root.
own.label: Verb in the infinitive
own.types_help: With a plural object, -a- is added after the root: exe-a-xati «he/she is seeing them». Write the meaning with «them»: «see them».

types.label: No object or a singular object

source.full: Ma. Guadalupe Hernández Dimas, Roberto Fabián Luis and Sereno Coló, Curso de lengua p'urhépecha (para no hablantes), notes from Fernando Nava's class, Instituto de Investigaciones Antropológicas, UNAM, 1998–1999; Alberto Medina Pérez, Guía lingüística p'urhépecha, Universidad Michoacana de San Nicolás de Hidalgo, 2006. See also: Paul P. de Wolf, Curso básico del tarasco hablado, El Colegio de Michoacán.

about: P'urhépecha (or Purépecha, also called Tarascan) is spoken in Michoacán: on the Meseta, around Lake Pátzcuaro, in the Cañada de los Once Pueblos and in the Ciénega de Zacapu. More than 140,000 people speak it.
It is a language isolate: it has no known relatives in Mexico or anywhere else in the Americas. It was the language of one of the great states of Mesoamerica, whose capital was Tzintzuntzan.
It is an agglutinative language and uses almost no prefixes: the verb grows by adding suffixes to the root, one after another. A single verb can have more than ten syllables.

orthography.intro: We use today's P'urhépecha alphabet: 6 vowels and 21 consonants. The apostrophe marks an aspirated consonant (with a puff of air), and ï is a central vowel, between i and u.
notes: No P'urhépecha word begins with b, d, g, ï, nh, r or rh, except loanwords from Spanish. B, d and g appear after m or n: témbeni, náandi, pirésïnga.
Every word ends in a vowel. If the last vowel isn't stressed, it is pronounced very weakly or almost not at all: uandani sounds almost like «uandan».
The written accent marks the stressed syllable and can change the meaning: karáni «write», kárani «fly». Books mostly write it on the verb root (piré-, uandá-).
Pronunciation is shown in brackets with the International Phonetic Alphabet (IPA).

grammar.intro: A P'urhépecha verb is built from left to right: the root and then, in order, the suffixes that say how the action unfolds, when, whether it is a statement or a question, and how many do it.

items.description: -xa now, -sïn by habit, -s done, -xam about to.
-p- past, -a future, -pirin conditional; nothing in the present.

blocks.title: The verb endings
blocks.description: They are added to the root. After m or n, ka and ti become ga and di: sïn + ka → sïnga.
blocks.note: The question forms work for every person: ¿uandaxaki? «is he/she speaking?», ¿uandaxakiksï? «are they speaking?».

blocks.title: The persons
blocks.description: Pronouns are hardly used: the verb already says who. To stress the subject, the pronoun or a clitic attached to the verb is used.
blocks.note: In the conjugator the singular clitics (-ni, -re) are not written; the plural ones are.

blocks.title: Four aspects
blocks.description: Before the tense, P'urhépecha says how the action unfolds. Each aspect has a present and a past.

examples.meaning: I am eating · I was eating

items.name: Habitual
items.description: What one does by habit, or knows how to do.

examples.meaning: I dance · I used to dance
I am about to sing · I was about to sing

blocks.title: Orders
blocks.description: The imperative is the bare root; in the plural, -e is added. To forbid, ásï goes before it, never «no». Ia adds «now, already».

blocks.title: Verbs with an irregular future
blocks.description: Jarhani, jurhani, nirani and a few others change rha or ra to u in the future, and in the conditional they keep only the first syllable.

examples.meaning: I will be · I would be
I will go · I would go
I will come · I would come

blocks.title: Plural object
blocks.description: When what receives the action is plural, the verb takes -a- after the root, and the noun takes -ni.

items.translation: How did you wake up? (good morning)

tenses.name: Present habitual
tenses.description: What one does by habit, or knows how to do (-sïn).

tenses.name: Past actual
tenses.description: What was happening when something interrupted it (-xap).

tenses.name: Past habitual
tenses.description: What one used to do and no longer does (-sïamp).

tenses.name: Imperative
tenses.description: The bare root; -e in the plural.
